https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/american-foo.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Brain scans of a former NFL player who was diagnosed with CTE By Michael Short BBC Sport senior journalist Published 6 hours ago As many as 97.7% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 could have had brain disease related to repeated blows to the head, a new study says. Researchers looked at 878 former players who died during that period, with 235 having donated their brains to research. Of those, 215 were found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease which can only be diagnosed after death. The study, published in the British Medical Journal , external , also found dementia was common among brain donors. "We and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," said the report's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School. "These findings indicate that NFL players have a higher prevalence of CTE at death than has been previously shown in multiple community based studies." Researchers calculated a "conservative minimum" of CTE prevalence among those who died in the six-year period to be 24.5% - rising to a "maximum" 97.7%. They have urged the NFL to take prevention measures to reduce repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport. Dallas Cowboys player who died by suicide diagnosed with brain disease Published 8 July NFL admits football-brain disease link Published 15 March 2016 New research finds link between head impacts & CTE Published 27 July 2022 "The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level," Danshvar said. "They occurred at the collegiate level and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk." An NFL spokesperson said: "The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. "The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust - and expanding - set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being. "We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health." CTE among American football players has been a growing issue in recent years. A 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement for the NFL limited the number of contact practices. Following a long-running class action, in 2016 the NFL agreed a $1bn (Â£700m) settlement with more than 5,000 former players. https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-mps-r.text: LONDON — British MPs threw out a bill legalizing assisted dying for terminally ill adults in England and Wales Friday. In a narrow vote, MPs rejected the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill's second reading by 286 to 270. The decision was a marked contrast to a near identical bill by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater, which received two votes of support from MPs in 2024 and 2025. The legislation failed to become law after running out of time in the unelected House of Lords earlier this year. Advertisement Advertisement The bill, introduced by backbench Labour MP Lauren Edwards , would have legalized assisted dying for adults aged 18 or over who are judged by two doctors as expected to die within six months. It will now make no further progress and follows members of the Scottish Parliament rejecting similar legislation in March and a previous vote by MPs against assisted dying in 2015. Assisted dying is currently illegal in the U.K. and assisting someone to end their life is punishable by up to 14 years in prison in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The vote was a matter of conscience, meaning parties did not whip their MPs who could vote as they wished. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was not an MP when Leadbeater's bill was previously debated, deliberately abstained to avoid swaying the views of MPs. Nonetheless, Burnham argued soon after becoming PM that fixing palliative and social care should come before legalizing assisted dying. “It is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care,” he said in July. Isabel Loubser contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

Fallon/AFP Advertisement The diesel deal between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin has sparked anger in Ukraine. Under the agreement, Moscow is allowed to supply Russian diesel fuel to global markets. The US news website Axios reported the move came in response to Kyiv's failure to comply with Washington's demands to stop attacks on oil refineries in Russia . Trump also declared that it was time "for Ukraine to get a new president." The agreement to sell diesel was announced while talks between Ukrainian, US and European representatives were taking place in Miami. "I think our team is simply being used as a cover. That is definitely not fair," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists shortly afterwards, describing Trump's decision as "a weak decision by strong partners." From the Oval Office to Miami This is hardly Kyiv's first crisis in its relationship with the Trump administration. In February 2025, Trump told Zelenskyy in the Oval Office "you don’t have the cards." The White House confrontation was followed by a suspension of weapons deliveries and intelligence-sharing agreements. According to media reports, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to suspend intelligence sharing during the talks in Miami, too, citing Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as the reason. US officials have denied the reports. Memories are rekindled of the February 2025 spat between Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Donald Trump and JD Vance Image: Jim Lo Scalzo/UPI Photo/IMAGO The current tension recalls the dispute in the White House at the time, says Mykhailo Honchar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" in an interview with DW. However, he says there is no reason for Ukrainians to panic. "Last year, too, there were threats and suspensions of intelligence sharing, as well as disruptions in weapons supplies," he said. "Then the Americans realized how much this was hurting them, too, and reluctantly resumed everything." Is Trump looking for a 'scapegoat?' All the experts interviewed by DW see a connection between Trump's threats toward Ukraine and the US midterm elections on November 3. In the midterms, all seats in the House of Representatives and roughly one third of Senate seats are up for election. Ivan Us of the National Institute for Strategic Studies in Kyiv expects a crushing defeat for the Republicans. He says the main reason will be high fuel prices. "Donald Trump wants desperately to distract attention from the fact that high prices are linked to his war with Iran and the problems in the Strait of Hormuz. He needs a scapegoat for this. And he has decided that Ukraine will be it," the expert said. Mykhailo Honchar sees Russia as the main beneficiary of Trump's deal with Putin: "This whole diesel deal looks like a disguised request from Putin to Trump to exert influence on Ukraine." Honchar also links the agreement to a possible sale of the foreign assets of Russian oil company Lukoil. According to The New York Times, potential buyers of these assets include investors with ties to Trump. Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? Oleksandr Kraiev of the Ukrainian think tank Ukrainian Prism warns against taking drastic action. "Slamming the door in anger will certainly not help us. In that case, security assistance and intelligence sharing will be off the table. We cannot afford that. It may be difficult, and sometimes even repulsive, but we have to maintain contact with the Americans," the expert said. At the same time, Ukraine could work with Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and France to make deliveries of Russian diesel fuel "simply unrealistic." After all, the tankers would have to pass through these countries' territorial waters on their way to the United States, and the partners have already said they would not allow this. Ivan Us advises against reading too much into the harsh rhetoric. "You can say whatever you want in public, as long as you carry on as before," he said of the possible relationship between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian diplomats should work with US Republicans and the MAGA movement. Trump's agreement with Putin is already being criticized in those circles, with some raising concerns that Russia could use the proceeds from the diesel trade to support Iran. Us also does not rule out a legal challenge to Trump's decision. Republican Senator Tom Tillis told NBC that the president was likely violating a 2022 law prohibiting imports of Russian oil and other energy products. Ivan Us considers US threats to cut Ukraine off from intelligence or weapons to be little more than "fearmongering" ahead of the elections. "The US makes such statements not because it intends to take action, but to make the markets believe that it is about to exert pressure and thereby drive prices down," Us said. What will change after November 3? The three experts agree that Kyiv should ride out the situation until after the US midterm elections on November 3. Oleksandr Kraiev says he is sure that Trump may back down on this issue after the elections, since abandoning Ukraine would mean showing weakness toward China. Mykhailo Honchar points out that Trump's deal with Putin is already being criticized by Republicans in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. In addition, Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick has introduced a bipartisan bill named after former US President Ronald Reagan that would block purchases of Russian oil. "Despite all the threats, and perhaps even some attempts to impose temporary measures against Kyiv, it is unlikely that Trump will go any further. The situation should not be portrayed in apocalyptic terms," Honchar said. He added that Trump's pressure was also bringing Ukraine and its European partners closer together.
